name: Thinkwell
line: Thinkwell teaches by video lecture in a set order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Thinkwell: Thinkwell teaches by video lecture, in a set order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Thinkwell teaches each lesson by video lecture, then exercises, in a set order, and assesses with quizzes, chapter tests, a midterm and a final [2]. In AMP, the problem is the unit. Each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer, and every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Thinkwell the unit is the lesson: a 5 to 10 minute video lecture by a university professor, then auto-graded exercises [2][5]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages. The data are correlational [9].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Thinkwell places a learner with a printable test and a scoring guide, and the result picks a course [3]. Inside the course, assessment is quizzes, chapter tests, a midterm and a final [2].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once, and repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Thinkwell, a wrong answer on an exercise brings a step-by-step explanation and a retry, as often as the learner likes, and the next lesson follows in the course's set order [2]. The course grade weights quizzes, chapter tests, a midterm and a final, and Thinkwell states no rule for when a single skill is learned [2].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Thinkwell's review is worksheets and study notes for each topic, plus practice exams, and its How it works page describes no schedule for bringing earlier skills back [2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [8].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, on one map of skills from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Thinkwell places a learner in one course, by a printed placement test [3].

rows.range: Single courses from grade 6 through calculus, with honors versions from grade 6 through Algebra 2 [1].
rows.start: A separate printable placement test with a scoring guide. The result picks a course [3].
rows.teaching: A 5 to 10 minute video lecture by a university professor, then auto-graded exercises with step-by-step explanations [2][5].
rows.next: The next lesson in the course's set order, on a suggested week-by-week plan the family can speed up or slow down [2].
rows.mastery: A course grade: quizzes and chapter tests at 30% each, the midterm and final at 20% each. No rule stated for single skills [2].
rows.review: Worksheets and study notes for each topic, plus practice exams. No schedule described for bringing earlier skills back [2].
rows.print: Printable worksheets with answer keys, and study notes for each topic. The same for every student [1][2].
rows.adult: Assigns the course, sets the pace, chooses the letter grade, and contacts support to allow a test retake [2].
rows.reports: An auto-graded online gradebook, a certificate and printed grades on request, and official transcripts sent to schools [2][4].
rows.evidence: None found on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][6][7].

theirs: Thinkwell makes video courses for homeschool learners. Its math runs from grade 6 through calculus, with honors versions from grade 6 through Algebra 2 [1]. University professors teach the lectures [5].

A learner starts with a printable placement test that picks a course [3]. Each lesson follows the same pattern: a 5 to 10 minute video, then auto-graded exercises with step-by-step explanations, which the learner can retry as often as they like. Printable worksheets and study notes are optional. Quizzes, chapter tests, a midterm and a final make up the grade, and a suggested week-by-week plan sets the pace, which the family can speed up or slow down [2].
credit: Lectures by university professors, with captions and printable transcripts [2][5].
Step-by-step explanations on its exercises, which a learner can retry as often as they like [2].
Courses through calculus, and honors versions from grade 6 through Algebra 2 [1].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Thinkwell on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][6][7].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages, in correlational data [9]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [8]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want a professor's video lecture before each set of exercises, in a course graded by quizzes, tests, a midterm and a final.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want printable workbooks made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Thinkwell?
questions.answer: Thinkwell places a learner with a printable test, teaches by video lecture in a set order, and grades with quizzes, tests, a midterm and a final [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Thinkwell work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Thinkwell on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][6][7].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
